--- Page 1 ---
From Questions to Decisions: Benchmarking How LLM Agents
Acquire Decision-Relevant Information from Human Beings
Yuhan Tang1∗, Ke Fan2∗, Xinkai Zou3∗, Baichuan Mo2†, Kangxin Cui4, Ao Qu1,
Ou Zheng5, Jiangbo Yu6, Xuan Jiang1, Haris N. Koutsopoulos7, Jinhua Zhao1‡, Yuan Zhou2‡
1Massachusetts Institute of Technology
2Tsinghua University
3University of California, San Diego
4Tongji University
5Peking University
6McGill University
7Northeastern University
Abstract
LLM agents are increasingly asked to make plans for peo-
ple, such as scheduling drivers or assigning nurses. However,
people’s requests are often incomplete, and the supporting
information for decision making may be outdated, requiring
agents to ask for clarification. Existing benchmarks typically
provide fully specified problems or rely on uncalibrated LLM-
simulated users, leaving this ability insufficiently tested. We
introduce Ask2Decide, a benchmark of 43 planning tasks
that evaluates whether agents ask for missing information that
matters for their decisions. An operator holds facts absent
from the agent’s request and records, and optimization solvers
determine which facts change the optimal plan. We also in-
clude similarly worded facts that leave the optimal plan un-
changed to test whether agents distinguish useful information
from irrelevant details. We collect 79 interaction sessions from
19 participants and find that, after an incorrect plan, human
replies omit the correcting fact far more often than replies
from an uncalibrated simulated user (43% versus 7%). Us-
ing these interactions, we calibrate a simulated operator that
more closely matches human reply patterns. Evaluating four
frontier LLMs, we find that their initial plans are infeasible on
58–98% of tasks when information is missing, compared with
5–28% when all facts are provided upfront. Agents uncover
facts that change the optimal plan only slightly more often
than facts that leave it unchanged (39–52% versus 32–41%).
These results show that obtaining decision-relevant informa-
tion through interaction remains a major bottleneck for LLM
planning. This is ongoing work and will be updated. The
date of this version is shown on the first page.
1
Introduction
LLM agents are increasingly asked to make plans for real-
world operations. Recent work has made progress in translat-
ing complete problem descriptions into optimization mod-
els (Ramamonjison et al. 2023; AhmadiTeshnizi, Gao, and
Udell 2024; Huang et al. 2025; Jiang et al. 2025). In prac-
tice, however, neither the initial request nor the organization’s
records describe the problem as it stands today. Some rules
were never written down; some conditions changed after the
∗These authors contributed equally.
†Corresponding author.
‡Senior authors.
records were made, through an accident, new information
or a system update not yet entered; and some records are
simply wrong. Those missing information could make the fi-
nal plans infeasible. A dispatcher asking for today’s delivery
routes may omit that one driver must return by 10:00. Assign-
ing that driver a longer route could make the plan infeasible.
Such conditions are known to the people involved but absent
from the request and the available records, so the agent can
learn them only from those people. Yet missing facts differ
in their consequences: some change which plan is feasible or
preferred, while others leave the decision unchanged. Effec-
tive planning therefore requires the agent to recognize what
it needs to know and direct its questions toward those facts.
This raises a question that current benchmarks do not answer:
can an agent elicit the missing information that matters for
its decision?
Existing evaluations fall short in two aspects. (1) They do
not measure the decision value of acquired information. Ex-
isting optimization evaluations focus on modeling and solv-
ing from fixed problem descriptions, without testing whether
agents uncover temporary changes in operational conditions.
Benchmarks for clarification and information acquisition ad-
dress missing information: QuestBench tests whether models
identify the clarification question needed to solve an under-
specified task (Li, Kim, and Wang 2025), while OR-Clarify
evaluates the recovery of withheld formulation requirements
before modeling (Ge et al. 2026). However, these evaluations
do not quantify the consequences of missing facts for plan
feasibility and solution quality, or evaluate the operational
plan produced after the interaction. This leaves open whether
agents acquire the information that matters for the decisions
they make. (2) Their simulated users do not reliably com-
municate as real human beings do. Interactive benchmarks
evaluate agents through conversations with LLM-simulated
users (Yao et al. 2025). Compared with real human beings,
default simulators produce overly verbose and polite replies,
exhibit less stylistic variation, and disclose information more
completely and earlier in the conversation (Dou et al. 2025;
Zhou et al. 2026). These differences can change how much
agents need to ask and yield success rates and failure patterns
that differ from human evaluations (Seshadri et al. 2026). Re-
liable evaluation therefore requires calibrating and validating

simulated responses against real human interactions.
To address both gaps, we introduce Ask2Decide, a bench-
mark for evaluating how agents acquire decision-relevant
information from people. It contains 43 planning tasks in
routing, scheduling, staffing and other domains. The agent
receives a brief and an incomplete knowledge base, and an
operator holds today’s hidden facts. Optimization makes a
good testbed because a solver can do two things exactly. It
computes the value of each hidden fact: its regret ∆is the
loss that the safest plan can still incur when the agent does
not know whether that fact holds, with the rest of the problem
fixed. And it scores any submitted plan against the true facts,
from 0 for an optimal plan to 1 for a plan that cannot be car-
ried out. Facts that change the plan (∆> 0) are paired with
twins: facts of the same form about another object that sound
just as important but leave the best plan unchanged. Figure 1a
shows such a pair. Recovering many facts is therefore not the
same as asking useful questions.
Table 1 runs the same planning agent (DeepSeek V4.1
Flash) on 22 tasks, once with the human operators of our
study (19 participants, 79 sessions) and once with a default
LLM operator (three runs per task). First, interactive plan-
ning is hard: with a full brief (every hidden fact in the first
message), the initial plan is rarely infeasible (3.0–6.3%), but
in the interactive condition, where the hidden facts are not
given, it is infeasible in 32.9–48.5% of episodes. Rejections
and revisions bring the final plan below 8%. Second, the op-
erator changes the result: the initial plan fails more often with
the default operator than with people, but the final plan fails
less often, because after a wrong plan the default operator
withholds the correcting fact in only 7% of replies, against
43% for people. We therefore build CalOp, a simulated oper-
ator calibrated on the human sessions, and Section 4 validates
it against them.
Because a solver can score every plan both with and with-
out the hidden facts, Ask2Decide can separate abilities that
a single success rate mixes together: modelling the problem,
asking for the facts that matter, and recovering after a rejected
plan. Since the operator is simulated, we also test how the
choice of operator changes these measurements. In Section 5
we use CalOp to evaluate four LLMs as the planning agent
on all 43 tasks and organize the results around four research
questions.
RQ1: How does access to complete information affect
initial-plan quality? Strongly. Models that plan well when
told every hidden fact produce an initial plan that cannot be
carried out on most tasks when those facts are not given. Ob-
taining the information, more than modelling the problem, is
the bottleneck.
RQ2: Do models ask about facts that change the plan?
Only weakly. Models uncover the facts that change the plan
barely more often than look-alike twins that do not, and on
large instances asking more questions does not rescue the
initial plan.
RQ3: How much do models recover after a rejected plan?
Much, but recovery hides how they asked. A rejection it-
self tells the agent that something is wrong today, and after
revisions, models that asked very differently end up close
together. We therefore score the initial plan for asking and
report the final plan as a measure of recovery.
RQ4: How does the choice of simulated operator affect
planning outcomes? It shifts individual scores in both direc-
tions but not the main conclusion: under both a default and
the calibrated operator, the interactive condition leaves far
more initial plans infeasible than a full brief.
In summary, our contributions are threefold:
• We introduce Ask2Decide, a benchmark of 43 planning
tasks in which an operator holds hidden facts that the
agent needs for its plan. Every hidden fact has an exact
or bounded regret label, matched zero-value twins serve
as controls, and the initial plan is scored under the true
conditions, so what an agent learns is tied to the quality
of its decision.
• We collect 79 operator sessions from 19 participants that
show how people release information. From these ses-
sions we build CalOp, a calibrated simulated operator,
and validate its reply form, factual faithfulness and plan-
ning outcomes against the human sessions. It matches
them more closely than a default LLM operator, so new
agents can be evaluated repeatedly without new human
dialogues.
• We evaluate four LLMs on all 43 tasks, comparing each
model’s initial plan with and without full hidden facts,
its uptake of relevant facts against twins, its initial plan
against its final plan, and two simulated operators. Even
the best model’s initial-plan loss rises from 0.03 when
told every hidden fact to 0.60 in the interactive condition,
and models uncover relevant facts only 5–11 points more
often than twins. Most of the loss comes from not asking
what matters, rather than from modelling.
2
Ask2Decide: Task Formulation
Ask2Decide measures whether an agent can ask people for
the information its decision depends on. When an LLM agent
helps a human being to make a decision, some of the facts
that matter are known only to that person: they are missing
from the request and from the records. A good agent does
not ask about everything. It finds the few facts that change
its decision.
An episode is one complete run of a task, from the initial
request to the evaluation of the submitted plans. It sepa-
rates three roles: the agent receives a request and incomplete
records, asks questions and submits plans; the operator holds
the missing facts and answers questions about specific ob-
jects; and the judge evaluates submitted plans against the true
conditions.

Figure 1: Overview of Ask2Decide on hard1_dialaride. (a) The agent gets a brief and the records, and the operator holds
today’s notes, each labelled by the solver with its regret ∆. The twin H5 has the same form as H2 but leaves the best plan

problem. Replies are constructed for illustration.
To make the value of a question measurable, we instantiate
the decision as an optimization problem. A solver can then
compute two things exactly: how much each missing fact can
change the best decision, and how good the final decision is
under the true facts. Whether a question was worth asking is
therefore computed by the solver, not judged by annotators.
Section 2.1 specifies what the agent, operator and judge
know and do, and describes how questions, plans and revi-
sions form an episode. Section 2.2 defines the loss of a plan
and the value of a hidden fact, the regret that can arise when it
remains unknown, and introduces twins as controls for facts
that leave the plan unchanged. Section 2.3 explains how plan
quality, information acquisition and recovery are measured,
and how comparison with complete information helps distin-
guish information acquisition from modelling. Section 3 then
describes how operational problems are turned into bench-
mark tasks by specifying the initial records and hidden facts,
adding controls and verifying their effects with a solver.
2.1
Setting
The three roles have different responsibilities and access to
information.
• The agent is the LLM under test, run in our planning
harness. It receives a short request from the operator, the
brief, and a knowledge base: the task’s existing records,
such as addresses, distances, time windows and vehicle
capacities. It can ask the operator questions, write a model
and solve it, and submit plans.
• The operator is a human participant or a simulated opera-
tor. It holds a few notes: facts about today that the records
do not show. Each note is one sentence about one object,
such as “vehicle 1 must be back at the depot by 10:00”. A
note may change a number in the records, take an object
out of use, add a rule the records leave out, or change
what the plan should optimize.
• The judge holds the true problem, that is, the knowledge
base with all notes applied. It checks every submitted plan
against this problem. The agent never sees the judge’s
result.
An episode runs as follows. The operator sends the brief,
which states the goal (“plan this morning’s rides, shortest
total distance”) but none of the notes. The agent then asks
questions and runs its solver. The operator may send at most
15 messages. The agent is told that its initial plan will be
carried out and scored, so it should ask before it plans. We
call this plan the initial plan. If the operator rejects it, the
agent may revise it up to twice. We call the last plan the final
plan and score it separately.
The operator answers only questions about a specific ob-
ject. Otherwise the agent could ask “any other constraints?”
and receive every note at once. Human participants are asked
to follow this rule. The simulated operator enforces it and
asks the agent to be more specific when a question covers
more than three objects.
Figure 1 shows an example: panel (a) gives what each side
knows, panel (b) one episode. The agent plans door-to-door
rides with two vehicles. The operator holds five notes (S1,
H2, H3, H4, H5). Only H2, H3 and S1 change the best plan.
H5 looks just like H2, but the same plan is best whether it
holds or not. Under this rule, “any other constraints?” reveals


--- Page 4 ---
nothing, while “when does vehicle 1 have to be back?” reveals
H2 and changes the plan, as in the episode of Figure 1b. The
rest of this section defines “changes the plan” precisely.
2.2
Plan Loss and the Value of a Fact
The tested agent sees a request, the records and the operator’s
answers, and it builds its own model from them. Behind
each task, however, we keep a reference model that only the
judge uses, and this model is what makes the value of a
fact computable. A plan is a decision written in the format
the task fixes, for example a route and a timetable for each
vehicle. Let X be the set of all such plans. A problem θ
specifies which plans are feasible, X(θ) ⊆X, and the cost
f(x; θ) of each plan. Its optimal value is
z(θ) =
min
x∈X(θ) f(x; θ).
(1)
We write everything for minimization. For maximization,
the differences below change sign. Every problem we solve
is feasible and has a nonzero optimal value.
Let H be the set of hidden items of a task. For S ⊆H, θS is
the problem obtained by starting from the agent’s knowledge
base and applying the true versions of the hidden items in S
only: every other hidden item keeps the value the knowledge
base gives it, and a rule the knowledge base lacks stays absent.
Thus θ∅is the problem exactly as the knowledge base states
it, before any note is applied, and θH is today’s true problem,
with every note applied. In Figure 1, vehicle 1 must be back
by 11:40 in θ∅and by 10:00 in θH. A hidden item can change
a number in the model (48% of all hidden items), take an
object out of use (18%), add a constraint (25%) or change
the objective (9%). θS is the problem an agent would face if
it had learned exactly the hidden items in S.
To score a plan x under a problem θ, the judge puts the
plan itself into θ:
ℓ(x; θ) =



x ∈X(θ).
(2)
An infeasible plan, or one not in the task’s format, lies outside
X(θ) and receives loss 1. Plans submitted in an episode
are scored under the true problem, ℓ(x; θH). A plan that
cannot be carried out loses everything; otherwise its loss is
the fraction by which it falls short of the best plan, capped
at 1. The judge computes f from the decision of the plan
proposed by the agent.
How much does it cost not to know a hidden item? An
agent that has not asked about h does not know which of
two problems it faces, the one without h or the one with
h, but it must still commit to one plan. Whatever h does,
whether it changes a number, takes an object out of use, adds
a constraint or changes the objective, it turns one problem
into the other. In Figure 1, H2 moves vehicle 1’s return from
11:40 to 10:00, and S1 adds a 25-minute ride limit that the
knowledge base lacks. A plan built for the problem without
h may fail or do badly in the problem with h; a plan built for
the problem with h may be worse than necessary if h does
not hold. The cost of not knowing h is the loss of the safest
plan, the one whose worse case is best. For a hidden item
h and a set S ⊆H \ {h} of other hidden items whose true
versions are known, we define the regret
∆h(S) = min
x∈X max

ℓ(x; θS), ℓ(x; θS∪{h})
	
,
(3)
known as minimax regret (Savage 1951). ∆h(S) = 0 when
one plan is optimal whether or not h holds, so asking about
h cannot improve the decision. A large ∆h(S) means that
every plan made without h can go badly wrong.
The regret depends on what else the agent already knows.
We report it at the two extremes,
∆sa
h = ∆h(∅),
∆cond
h
= ∆h(H \ {h}).
(4)
The standalone regret ∆sa
h measures how much h matters to
an agent that knows only the records; the conditional regret
∆cond
h
measures how much it matters to an agent that knows
every other hidden item, so that its two problems are today’s
true problem θH and θH with only h reverted to the records.
Often the regret can be read off the two optimal values.
Suppose h leaves the objective unchanged and only removes
feasible plans, X(θS∪{h}) ⊆X(θS), as an added or tight-
ened constraint or an object taken out of use does. Then
∆h(S) = min
n
1, z(θS∪{h}) −z(θS)
|z(θS)|
o
.
(5)
A plan infeasible under θS∪{h} has loss 1 there. A plan
feasible under it costs at least z(θS∪{h}) in both problems,
so its loss under θS is at least the ratio in Eq. 5, and the
optimal plan of θS∪{h} attains this bound. When h only
adds feasible plans, the same holds with the two problems
swapped. In both cases the regret is the relative gap between
the two optimal values, measured against the optimum of the
less constrained problem.
In two situations, however, Eq. 5 does not hold, and the
regret must be computed from Eq. 3 directly. When h moves
a time window, neither feasible set contains the other. When
h changes the objective, the optimal value can change al-
though the optimal plan does not. In the candy-blending
task (medium6_candy_blend), today’s optimal profit is
$2800. Without the true glucose-syrup price it would be
$3250, and without the true maltose price $5110. Both prices
lower the optimal profit, but the glucose-syrup price leaves
the optimal blend unchanged, so its conditional regret is 0:
the lower profit is a cost no plan can avoid, not a consequence
of not asking. The maltose price changes the blend, and its
conditional regret is 0.093. We therefore compute every label
from Eq. 3. Where an optimum is not proved (frontier-B),
solver bounds turn the label into an interval (Appendix B).
We call a hidden item relevant if ∆sa
h > 0 or ∆cond
h
>
0. The two regrets can order hidden items differently. In
Figure 1, H2 has ∆sa = 0.353 but ∆cond = 0.007: once
the other hidden items are known, it changes the plan only
slightly. S1, the 25-minute ride limit, shows the opposite: it
does not matter on its own (∆sa = 0) but has ∆cond = 0.141
when the other hidden items hold. A twin is a hidden item of
the same form as a relevant one but about another object, with
both regrets zero. H5 (vehicle 2 back by 10:40) is the twin
of H2: it sounds just as important, yet one plan is optimal
whether or not it holds. An agent that asks about everything


--- Page 5 ---
collects both, while an agent that reasons about its plan asks
about H2. Not every hidden item with zero regret is a twin:
H4 (Peter has a companion) has no relevant counterpart.
2.3
Evaluation Metrics
A single score for the whole episode would mix three abili-
ties: building and solving a correct model, asking for the facts
that matter, and recovering after a rejected plan. A poor final
plan could come from a failure in any of them. We therefore
score the episode at a fixed point, add a control without any
missing information, and measure asking directly.
The main score is the loss of the initial plan. Let x1 be the
initial plan an agent submits in an episode and xfin its last
one. The initial-plan loss is ℓ(x1; θH) (Eq. 2): 1 if the plan
cannot be carried out in today’s true problem, and otherwise
its optimality gap, capped at 1. Like the quality–yield index
for generated heuristics (Chen et al. 2026a), it folds feasibility
and quality into one number, so we also report two parts of
it separately: the infeasible rate, the share of tasks with x1 /∈
X(θH), and the optimal rate, the share with ℓ(x1; θH) = 0.
We score the initial plan because it is the only one made
before any feedback. A rejection itself tells the agent that
something is wrong, so later plans reflect trial and error
rather than asking. The final-plan loss ℓ(xfin; θH) is reported
separately as a measure of recovery. All scores are averaged
over tasks.
A high initial-plan loss does not yet say whether the agent
failed to ask or failed to model and solve. To separate the two,
we run every task in a second condition. In the interactive
condition described so far, the hidden items are available
only from the operator. In the all-info condition, the agent
is given every hidden item together with the request and the
knowledge base, so it starts from today’s true problem. There
is no operator, and it submits a single plan xall. Its all-info
loss ℓ(xall; θH) measures how well the agent models and
solves when nothing is missing. The asking gap is the initial-
plan loss minus the all-info loss, computed per task and then
averaged. It is the part of the loss that comes from the hidden
information. Both plans are made before any feedback, so
the comparison is fair.
Neither loss shows which facts the agent went after. For
this we use the twins as controls. For a task, let R be its
relevant hidden items, T its twins and D the hidden items
the operator has disclosed before the initial plan. The relevant
recall is |D ∩R|/|R| and the twin rate is |D ∩T|/|T|. Both
are averaged over the tasks that have relevant hidden items
and twins. A twin reads just as important as its relevant
counterpart, so an agent that does not reason about its plan
learns both at about the same rate, and a gap between the two
shares shows a preference for facts that matter. The operator
also discloses notes it was not asked about, so we report a
stricter version in which D contains only the hidden items
that one of the agent’s questions was about, as judged by the
operator. Finally, we report the number of questions the agent
asks before its initial plan.
3
Benchmark Construction
We build each task from an optimization instance and a set of
hidden operational facts. The construction specifies the re-
Category
Example from the task suite

omit: “our vans hold 60 crates at most” (S#;
constraint).
Sudden accident
“One truck broke down this morning, so we
can run 3 truck trips at most today” (value);
“the road from warehouse 1 to warehouse 4
is closed today” (availability).
New information
“The hotel chain ordered 600 kg of Value
candy” (constraint); “CA1502 picked up a
tailwind, now expected at 08:15” (objective).
System update
“The grid company has new ramping rules:
at most 20 MW an hour” (constraint); a price
change this week (objective).
Human error
A record nobody updated: “C07’s certificate
for routine nursing checks has lapsed” while
the records still list C07 for them (availabil-
ity).
Table 2: The five categories of hidden information. Paren-
theses give each example’s effect on the model.
quest and records available to the agent, the additional facts
held by the operator, and the complete problem used by the
judge to score plans. As shown from left to right in Figure 2,
the four steps prepare the records and checker, introduce
hidden items and controls, compute their value labels, and
validate their effects on the plan. Together, these steps pro-
vide operational hidden information, solver-computed val-
ues, matched controls and a verifiable outcome.
First, a task starts from an optimization instance: a
textbook problem, Solomon’s r101 vehicle-routing in-
stance (Solomon 1987), or an instance from FrontierOR,
ORAgentBench, OR-Library or MIPLIB (Kong et al. 2026;
Li et al. 2026; Beasley 1990; Gleixner et al. 2021). Its data
are written as the knowledge base, the operator’s brief states
the goal, and a task-specific checker scores any plan under
the true specification. This step secures a verifiable outcome.
Second, the author writes the hidden items. They are not
drawn at random. Each one is a fact of a kind that working
operators hold and records miss. Table 2 sorts the hidden
information into five kinds: basic information that was never
written down, sudden accidents, new information that arrived
after the records were made, system updates not yet reflected
in the records, and human errors in the records. The kind
says why the records miss a hidden item. It is independent
of the item’s effect on the model, defined in Section 2.2, and
the table tags each example with that effect. Hidden items are
written for specific objects of the instance, so that the agent
can reach each one with a specific question. Some hidden
items get twins of the same form about other objects. The
frontier tasks generate both from shared templates. This step
secures operational hidden information: each hidden item is
a fact about today or an unwritten rule, not a missing piece
of a formulation template.
Third, for every hidden item, the solver computes the stan-
dalone and conditional labels of Eq. (3). A hidden item’s
kind says how it could arise in practice, while its label says
whether it changes the plan. Because the labels are com-

Figure 2: How a task is built (dial-a-ride example). Steps 1–2 are written by the task author, or by a script for the frontier splits.
Steps 3–4 are run by the solver. Below each step: the design criterion it secures.
puted, this step secures computed value, and checking that
twins come out at zero secures matched controls.
Fourth, the construction checks whether plans that are
optimal under incomplete knowledge remain optimal today.
A solver bound can exclude all such plans, whereas checking
one stored solution shows only that this solution fails. If an
optimal plan survived without the relevant hidden items, the
agent could do well without asking.
Table 3 summarizes the 43 tasks, which come in five splits
of growing size. Its item counts include the missing rules
(S#), and Appendix A lists every task.
• Easy, medium and hard (24 tasks) are textbook-size prob-
lems that a solver handles in seconds. They differ in how
much modelling the agent must do and how the hidden
items interact. In easy tasks the knowledge base lists six
or seven candidate plans, so the agent only has to pick
one. Two hidden items change the plan. In medium tasks
the agent writes a small LP or MILP itself (transporta-
tion, assignment, covering, cutting). Two or three hidden
items change the plan, each with a twin. Hard tasks are
routing and scheduling problems (dial-a-ride, job shop,
unit commitment, crew duties), in which the value of one
hidden item depends on what else is known and a missed
item often makes the plan infeasible.
• The frontier splits (19 tasks) are larger problems with
many named objects (flights, vessels, trips, work orders,
clients), built by a scripted pipeline. In frontier-A (17
tasks) offline solves prove optimality, so every ∆is exact.
The agent itself works under a shorter online run limit.
In frontier-B (2 tasks) offline solves do not close, so ∆is
a certified interval and plans are scored against the best
known solution rather than a proved optimum.
4
From Human Operators to a Calibrated
Simulated Operator
Evaluating an agent needs an operator who answers it many
times, over many tasks and seeds. People are too costly for
every run, and, as Table 1 shows, a default LLM operator
answers unlike people. We call this baseline DefaultOp: a
single prompt that gives an LLM the notes and the answer-
ing protocol. We therefore record how people play the op-
erator, build from these records CalOp, a human-calibrated

simulated operator, and check it against both people and De-
faultOp. Figure 3 shows the whole design.
Operator study.
In deployment, the operator is a domain
expert who knows today’s facts without looking them up. Our
participants cannot be experts in every task domain, so we
give them what such an expert would carry in mind: hidden
information notes, a check of each plan against the true condi-
tions, and an optional hinter that points to the note a question
concerns. These aids, shown in Figure 3a, spare participants
from working out the task themselves, so that they can an-
swer as readily as an expert would. Every participant plays
the operator of one task on a web app. They see the brief and
the notes, answer the planning agent (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash)
in their own words, and accept or reject its plans. Under the
answering protocol they answer only questions about a spe-
cific object. Nineteen participants completed 79 sessions on
22 tasks, giving 321 operator replies. Appendix C describes
the interface.
How people answer.
Table 4 shows three regularities. (1)
People are terse: a reply has 24.2 characters on average,
not counting spaces and punctuation, against 35.1 for De-
faultOp. (2) They answer what is asked: a reply discloses
about 1.4 notes. (3) After a wrong plan they often say only
that it is wrong: 43% of such replies reject or hint without
stating the correcting fact, against 7% for DefaultOp. The
last point matters most for evaluation, because a rejection that
carries the fact lets an agent repair its plan without asking.
CalOp.
CalOp reproduces these regularities with three
steps per turn and two LLM calls. As Figure 3b shows, it
takes the participant’s place in the same loop. (1) Policy. Code

calibrate CalOp on the human replies and validate it against them (Table 4)
Figure 3: Study design. (a) People play the operator against a solver-equipped planning agent; the agent asks and plans, the
person answers and accepts or rejects plans, and every exchange is logged. (b) The logs calibrate CalOp, which takes the
person’s place in the same loop, so that any LLM can be evaluated without new human sessions. Orange: LLM components;
teal: people and data; blue: solver.
samples the turn’s behavior from the rates of the development
participants: the reaction to a plan (accept, reject, hint or
correct), whether to answer in a word or two, the maximum
number of facts, a length target, and whether to number
the answers. (2) Content. An LLM call selects the notes
that the message literally asks about. A changed fact about
an object the agent names must be stated, with numbers
verbatim. A rejection targets a note flagged by the plan check.
(3) Wording. A second LLM call writes the reply at the target
length, using real replies from other tasks as style examples.
Both LLM calls use DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with thinking off,
as does DefaultOp. Unlike earlier variants (Appendix D),
CalOp keeps no per-participant profile.
Validation.
A simulated operator is useful only if it can
stand in for a person, so we check three things in turn: does
it answer like a person, does it answer correctly, and does an
agent reach similar plans with it as with a person? Table 4 has
one block per question and compares CalOp and DefaultOp
with the human column. For the first (block a), we give
CalOp the same conversation as each of the 321 human
replies, let it write its own reply, and compare its replies with
the human ones on 11 measures such as length, the number
of notes disclosed and how often the fact is withheld after a
wrong plan (Appendix E). Averaged over the measures, its
gap to people is about half that of DefaultOp (0.213 vs.
0.395), and the largest difference disappears: after a wrong
plan, people withhold the fact in 43% of replies, CalOp in
48% and DefaultOp in only 7%. For the second (block b),
we ask CalOp about single notes and let a scripted agent ask
about every note in turn: 1.1% of its answers are wrong or
invented, and the scripted agent reaches the optimal plan on
21 of 22 tasks. For the third (block c), the planning agent
of the study talks to each simulated operator on the same 22
tasks, three times per task. The final plans are about as good as
with people (loss 0.100 with CalOp, 0.117 with people and

5
Experiments
5.1
Experimental Setting
Tasks and models.
We evaluate four LLMs on all 43 tasks:
GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 3.8 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and
GLM-5.3 Flash. Each model acts as the agent in the same
planning harness and calls Gurobi through a solver service.
CalOp plays the operator in the main evaluation.
Conditions.
We run each model in two conditions. In the
interactive condition, the hidden facts are available only from
the operator. In the all-info condition, the agent receives


--- Page 8 ---
every hidden item up front and submits one plan without
an operator. This tells us how well it plans once nothing is
missing. All-info is compared only with the initial interactive
plan, which is also made before any feedback, so it needs no
chance to revise. To test the operator itself, we fix DeepSeek
V4.1 Flash as the model, use the 24 easy, medium and hard
tasks, and compare the interactive condition with a full-brief
condition: the operator gives every hidden item in its first
message and still reacts to plans, so both conditions allow the
same revisions. Each runs with CalOp and with DefaultOp,
giving four conditions and 96 episodes.
Protocol.
Each episode allows at most 15 operator mes-
sages and three plans. Only the initial plan counts for the
benchmark score. Later plans measure recovery. The agent
is told this in the interactive condition, and is told that it
has three attempts in the full-brief condition. Both operators
follow the same answering protocol, and a check makes sure
their replies agree with the notes. The judge scores each plan
on the true problem and never shows the score to the agent.
All runs use seed 0 and a solver budget of two threads and
300 seconds.
Metrics.
We use the metrics of Section 2.3. For the initial
plan, we report loss, the infeasible rate and the optimal rate,
together with all-info loss and the asking gap. For asking, we
report relevant recall, twin rate and the number of questions
before the initial plan. For recovery, we report the same scores
for the final plan. Intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals over
tasks.
5.2
How does access to complete information
affect initial-plan quality?
A model can fail a task for two reasons: it cannot model and
solve the problem, or it does not learn the facts the problem
depends on. To tell the two apart, we compare each model’s
initial plan in the interactive condition with its initial plan in
the all-info condition. If the two are close, asking is not the
bottleneck; if the first is much worse, the loss comes from
what the model did not find out.
Table 5 reads from left to right. Block (a) is the bench-
mark score: the initial plan a model submits in the interac-
tive condition. Block (b) shows where the model ends after
feedback, which RQ3 discusses. Block (c) gives the same
model’s initial-plan loss when it is told every hidden item,
and the asking gap, the part of the loss that comes from the
hidden information. Complete information substantially im-
proves every model’s initial plan. Told every hidden item, the
models reach an initial-plan loss of 0.03–0.26; in the inter-
active condition, it rises to 0.60–0.98. For every model, the
asking gap (0.56–0.81) is larger than the all-info loss, so the
hidden information costs more than modelling and solving.
Even the strongest model, GPT-6.1 Sol, returns an initial plan
that cannot be carried out on 58% of tasks in the interactive
condition. Most of the loss thus comes from plans that fail
outright, not from plans that are merely suboptimal.
Table 6 breaks the comparison down by split and shows
two sources of difficulty. On easy and medium tasks, all-info
loss is almost zero: the models can model and solve these
problems, and the loss under interaction comes from not
finding out the facts. On frontier-A, some models still lose
much when told every fact (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 0.59), so
modelling and solving are also a bottleneck there. The asking
gap should therefore be read together with the all-info loss.
A small gap can mean that the model asks well and does well
in both conditions, as GPT-6.1 Sol does on easy tasks (0.18
interactive, 0.00 all-info), or that it does poorly in both, as
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash does on frontier-A (1.0 and 0.59).
5.3
Do models ask about facts that change the
plan?
A model that knows what matters should learn the relevant
hidden items more often than their twins, which look just
as important but leave the plan unchanged. A model that
simply asks broadly should learn both at about the same
rate. We therefore compare, before the initial plan, the share
of relevant items a model learned (relevant recall) with the
same share for twins (twin rate). Table 7 counts an item in
two ways. Disclosed counts every item the operator stated,
including facts it volunteered; asked about counts only items
that one of the model’s questions targeted, so that a lucky
answer does not count as good asking.
Models prefer relevant items only weakly. For the three
models that ask regularly, relevant recall exceeds the twin
rate by 5–12 percentage points under either count. GLM-5.3
Flash asks almost no questions and learns almost nothing.
On the large tasks the preference disappears. On frontier-
A, all three models are told twins at least as often as relevant
items, and counting only what they asked about, the two
shares differ by at most 4 points. This is not for lack of
asking: Table 6 shows that GPT-6.1 Sol asks 11.2 questions
per episode on frontier-A, more than on any textbook split,
yet learns only 37% of the relevant items. Asking more is
therefore not the same as asking the right questions. With
a limited number of messages, the hard part is to work out
which missing facts could change the plan and to ask about
those first.
5.4
How much do models recover after a rejected
plan?
Feedback helps every model. Comparing blocks a and b of
Table 5, after at most two revisions the loss falls from 0.60–
0.98 for the initial plan to 0.42–0.62 for the final one. Table 6
shows that most of the gain comes from the smaller tasks:
on easy and medium tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 3.8 Flash
and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash end with a final loss of at most
0.13, while on frontier-A all four models stay at 0.77–0.82.
Feedback thus repairs plans when the model can solve the
problem but missed some facts, but does little when the
problem itself is too hard.
Recovery, however, says little about asking. A rejection
tells the agent that something about today is wrong, and
often which plan element broke, so a model can fix its plan
without having asked well. GLM-5.3 Flash shows this most
clearly: it asks 0.6 questions per episode, yet its loss falls
from 0.98 to 0.62 after rejections. Likewise, GPT-6.1 Sol,
Gemini 3.8 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash start far apart
(0.60–0.82) but end close together (0.42–0.45). A final-plan

5.5
How does the choice of simulated operator
affect planning outcomes?
Table 8 shows that replacing DefaultOp with CalOp
produces mixed changes in planning outcomes. Although
CalOp better matches the observed human reply statistics in
Table 4, it yields more optimal final plans and also higher
mean final loss. This combination is possible because loss
penalizes infeasibility heavily. A small number of infeasible
plans can outweigh gains in optimality elsewhere. The two
metrics therefore reveal different aspects of the outcome dis-
tribution, and neither operator consistently gives the planning
agent an advantage across the reported measures.
The much larger contrast is between asking for information
and receiving the full brief. Under either operator, provid-
ing the notes up front makes feasible initial plans common,
whereas interaction leaves many initial plans infeasible. The
information gap thus persists across the two simulators. Both
share code-enforced answering rules, which may constrain
their behavioral differences, although isolating that effect
would require an ablation. The differing instructions about
revisions also limit a causal interpretation of the information

comparison.
These results support evaluating operator behavior and
planning outcomes together. Reply statistics describe how
information is released, while the plan metrics measure
how an agent performs within that interaction. In this one-
model, one-seed control, a matched human condition would
be needed to determine how either simulator changes scores
relative to human interaction.
6
Related Work
Table 9 places Ask2Decide among related benchmarks
along five properties: whether information is withheld from
the agent, whether people played the answering role, whether
the agent’s plan or solution is scored, how the value of a
missing item is defined, and whether zero-value controls are
included.
Clarification and information seeking.
QuestBench (Li,
Kim, and Wang 2025) casts missing information as an un-
derspecified constraint satisfaction problem with one miss-
ing variable. Active task disambiguation (Kobalczyk et al.
2025) and EVPI-based question ranking (Rao and Daumé III
2018) choose questions by expected information value. Ask-
before-Plan (Zhang et al. 2024) studies clarification in travel
planning. Closest to us, OR-Clarify (Ge et al. 2026) hides for-
mulation slots of optimization problems, grades their severity
by annotation, and checks with an LLM judge whether they
were recovered. We hide numerical and rule information as
well, assign regret labels that are exact or bounded, include
∆= 0 controls, and score submitted plans under the true task

Table 9: Comparison with related benchmarks.
conditions. Drossman, Jacquillat, and Martin (2026) study
conversational refinement of a solution with LLM stakehold-
ers. Collaborative Battleship (Grand et al. 2026) is closest in
method: it collects human games, compares human and LM
askers, and scores questions by expected information gain
(EIG) about the hidden board. EIG values information about
the state; our ∆values information about the decision, and
the twins are hidden items with information about the state
but none about the decision. Its finding that high-EIG ques-
tions alone do not raise game performance is in line with our
separation of asking and planning.
LLMs for optimization modelling.
NL4Opt, OptiMUS,
ORLM, LLMOPT and OptMATH (Ramamonjison et al.
2023; AhmadiTeshnizi, Gao, and Udell 2024; Huang et al.
2025; Jiang et al. 2025; Lu et al. 2025) assume a com-
plete problem statement. Our tasks reuse such instances (e.g.
IndustryOR) and remove information. OPT-Engine (Chen
et al. 2026b) scales instance size under full information and
finds that added non-canonical constraints, rather than word-
ing or objective changes, cause most failures. Our hidden
notes are such constraints, held back. HeuriGym (Chen et al.
2026a) scores LLM-written heuristics by feasibility and qual-
ity against expert solutions in a feedback loop. We score plans
in the same way but withhold part of the problem.
Simulated users.
τ-bench (Yao et al. 2025) and its succes-
sors evaluate agents against LLM-simulated users. Compar-
isons with real users find simulators over-cooperative and
stylistically uniform, inflating agent success (Zhou et al.
2026; Seshadri et al. 2026; Dou et al. 2025; Wang et al.
2025). We calibrate the operator on human sessions from the
same tasks and validate it on the benchmark outcome.
7
Discussion and Conclusion
Implications for agents.
The results point to three open
problems. (1) Deciding what to ask. Told every hidden item,
the models reach an initial-plan loss of 0.03–0.26; in the
interactive condition, it rises to 0.60–0.98, and they learn
relevant items only 5–12 points more often than twins. Ask-
ing more does not fix this: on frontier-A, GPT-6.1 Sol asks
11.2 questions per episode and is still told twins as often
as relevant items. The solver that scores a plan could also
rank candidate questions, as expected information gain ranks
questions in information-seeking games (Grand et al. 2026).
A regret-guided asker is a natural baseline. (2) Solving at
scale. On frontier-A, some models lose much even when
told everything (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 0.59), so modelling
large instances remains a second bottleneck. (3) Evaluating
the initial plan. A rejection tells the agent that something
is wrong, so final plans move close together (0.42–0.45 for
three models), even for a model that hardly asks. Benchmarks
of interactive planning should score the plan made before any
feedback and report the final plan separately, as recovery.
Conclusion.
We introduced Ask2Decide, a benchmark of
43 planning tasks in which an operator holds hidden facts
the agent needs, a solver labels the value of every fact, and
the plan is scored under the true conditions. From 79 human
sessions we built CalOp, a simulated operator that answers
like people, including withholding the correcting fact after
a wrong plan, which a default LLM operator almost never
does. Evaluating four LLMs, we find that current models
can solve a fully stated problem but rarely find out what the
problem is: their initial plan cannot be carried out on 58–98%
of tasks in the interactive condition, and they barely prefer
the facts that matter over look-alikes that do not. Feedback
hides much of this gap, so the initial plan is what measures
asking. We hope Ask2Decide helps to build agents that ask
what matters.

A
Task inventory and cards
The following inventory and English task-card export were
generated from repository snapshot ba6dbd5. Counts use
only the displayed notes, not spare answer-key items. An ex-
act positive conditional label is relevant; for an interval, its
lower bound must be positive. The two frontier hidden items
below 0.005 remain included: x_warehouse/H2 (0.0032)
and x_watch/S1 (0.0039). The export preserves recorded
labels and outcome descriptions. It is not a new solver certi-
fication. In Table 3, Rel. counts positive conditional labels,
using positive lower bounds for interval labels. No 0.005
threshold is applied. Twins are the stored irrelevant
controls. Nine other hidden items have zero conditional value
and are not in that control category.
Effect of each hidden item on the model.
We tagged every
displayed hidden item by what it changes in the model, using
its recorded model change and the task’s knowledge base: a
value the records hold, the availability of an object or option,
a new constraint, or the objective. Over all 235 hidden items
the counts are 112 / 43 / 58 / 21, and one hidden item (a twin
in easy1_dispatch) changes nothing in the model. By
split (value / availability / constraint / objective): easy 16 / 5
/ 7 / 3, medium 15 / 7 / 3 / 12, hard 31 / 5 / 13 / 6, frontier-A
46 / 26 / 29 / 0, frontier-B 4 / 0 / 6 / 0. Of the 27 S# hidden
items, 25 add a constraint and 2 tighten a value the records
already hold. Twins and the other notes have similar profiles
(other notes 64 / 25 / 13 / 11, twins 46 / 18 / 20 / 10), so a
twin cannot be told apart by the kind of change it makes.

--- Page 14 ---
B
Computing regret labels
Each label is ∆h(S) from Eq. 3. It compares two problems,
θS and θS∪{h}, that differ only in the hidden item h being
tested: the standalone label uses S = ∅, so every other hidden
item keeps its knowledge-base value, and the conditional
label uses S = H \ {h}, so every other hidden item is at
its true value. When h leaves the objective unchanged and
only removes or only adds feasible plans, the label follows
from the two optimal values by Eq. 5. Otherwise, when h
changes the objective or moves a time window, we solve one
more optimization problem, of the same type as the task’s
own model: it looks for a single plan that is feasible in both
problems and minimizes the larger of its two losses. If no
plan is feasible in both, the label is 1. Some earlier tasks
record more than two plausible values for a hidden item; the
maximum in Eq. 3 then runs over the problems for all of them.
Exact labels require proved optima. If a solve remains open,
solver bounds give a regret interval. A zero label applies to
the background in which it was checked, rather than to every
possible knowledge state.
The frontier tasks generate twins from shared templates.
The earlier tasks also contain less strictly matched irrelevant
notes, such as H4 in Figure 1. We count only the stored
irrelevant controls as twins. All of them have zero standalone
and zero conditional regret. We do not assume that every
relevant hidden item has its own twin.
C
Human study and assistance
The selected data contain 79 completed protocol sessions.
They cover 22 tasks. The 321 replies are split by participant:
nine participants and 161 replies in development, ten partic-
ipants and 160 replies in test. The human data do not include
hard1_dialaride or hard2b_r101_25. Figure 1 is
therefore an illustrative task, not a transcript excerpt.
Participants see a brief and hidden notes, answer the plan-
ning agent, and accept or reject its plans. The app disables
ordinary paste actions. Each plan card can show a check un-
der the true task conditions. The optional Hinter can explain
which question to answer and, in the checked implementa-
tion, can state a numeric answer from the notes or reference.
It must not disclose the reference optimum as an answer.
The planning agent does not receive the participant’s private
plan-check display directly.
Each session allows up to 15 messages and three plans. The
planning agent can call a solver: it sends a model and PuLP
code, and each plan must state the result of its latest optimal
run. Measured on the raw text with whitespace removed, the
median human reply has 15 characters and 40.8% of replies
contain no punctuation. The 24.2-character mean in Table 4
instead excludes spaces and punctuation.
The historical study uses sandboxed Python/PuLP with
CBC and a 60-second solve limit. The main benchmark in-
stead uses the Gurobi service described in the experimental
setup. These settings must not be treated as identical.
D
Operator design and earlier variants
The selected f_min4 operator samples reply behavior from
population statistics and separates content selection from
wording.
Earlier variants added per-person profiles, calibration,
style controls and additional checks. The pooled replay dis-
tances are 0.395 for default, 0.350 for pc2s, 0.339 for
f_v5, 0.289 for f_v6, 0.242 for f_v7, and 0.213 for
f_min4. These are comparisons among developed systems,
not controlled estimates of the causal effect of removing
each component. They also do not establish which version
best represents a new participant population.
The planning benchmark adds an object-enumeration
guard and a truth-check wrapper. The historical operator
validation does not measure the combined effect of these
components. The historical probe results show that f_min4
is imperfect: its oracle loop succeeds on 21 of 22 tasks. The
failure involves an answer that names a football match with-
out stating that the person cannot attend.
In the full-brief comparison, the operator instructions still
describe the notes as private even though the agent receives
them. This limits interpretation of that comparison.
E
Evaluator definitions and uncertainty
The 11 replay measures are character count, sentence count,
colloquial rate, structured-answer rate, information-point
count, information density, extra-information ratio, hidden
notes disclosed, the share of replies that disclose at least two
notes, repetition rate, and withholding after a wrong plan.
Character count excludes spaces and punctuation. Informa-
tion density is 100 times the number of information points
divided by that count. The semantic annotations use a fixed
model judge and rubric. They are not human ground truth.
The historical evaluator reports 5,816 annotated replies out
of 5,827 across its selected sources. Metric sample counts
differ when an annotation or denominator is missing.
For metric m, let am and hm be the operator and human
group means. The pooled distance is
D = 1

This summary can hide distributional and per-participant
differences. Paired reply errors are separate metrics. A de-
velopment/test split alone does not turn the pooled summary
into held-out validation.
For closed-loop outcomes, we average sessions or seeds
within a task and then average the 22 task means. Because
every task has equal weight, these rates differ slightly from
the per-session rates in Table 1. The table below uses 20,000
percentile bootstrap samples of those task means, with boot-
strap seed 20261101. These intervals condition on the ob-
served participants and runs. They do not capture participant-
population uncertainty. Historical optimality means a feasi-
ble plan with relative gap at most 0.001.
For the main evaluation in Tables 5 and 7, the task-
bootstrap 95% intervals are: initial-plan loss GPT-6.1 Sol
[0.46, 0.74], Gemini 3.8 Flash [0.67, 0.91], DeepSeek V4.1
Flash [0.70, 0.93], GLM-5.3 Flash [0.94, 1.00]; relevant re-
call (disclosed) GPT-6.1 Sol [42%, 63%], Gemini 3.8 Flash
